summary: Defines an additional iSCSI node name type format that uses the T11 Network Address Authority (NAA) worldwide naming format. iSCSI maps the SCSI protocols onto TCP/IP. It was replaced by RFC 7143.

eli5.summary: Storage devices need unique names. This memo adds a way to reuse an existing worldwide naming system for them. A newer document replaced it.

questions: what is naa format for iscsi
can iscsi use fibre channel names
how do mixed storage transports name devices
subtitle: Using worldwide Fibre Channel names for iSCSI storage devices.

tldr.problem: Storage devices often have both SAS (Serial Attached SCSI) and iSCSI ports. SAS uses the NAA worldwide naming format, but iSCSI originally did not support it, forcing administrators to manage separate names for the same device.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3980 defines a new iSCSI node name type, `naa.`, that lets iSCSI nodes be identified using the same NAA format as Fibre Channel and SAS devices. An NAA identifier is represented as ASCII-encoded hexadecimal.
tldr.outcome: Storage devices with mixed protocols can now use a single NAA identifier as their device name across all transports, simplifying administration and naming consistency.

today: RFC 3980 was superseded by RFC 7143, the updated iSCSI specification. The NAA naming format for iSCSI remains valid and supported by modern implementations.

sections.title: Why NAA for iSCSI
sections.content:
iSCSI is a way to send SCSI storage commands over TCP/IP. It allows a computer to access remote storage as if it were local.

Storage devices often have multiple ports using different transports: Fibre Channel (FC), Serial Attached SCSI (SAS), and iSCSI. FC and SAS both use the NAA (Network Address Authority) format from the INCITS T11 standards, which provides a worldwide unique identifier. iSCSI originally supported only the IQN (iSCSI Qualified Name) format, which was different.

This RFC adds support for NAA names in iSCSI, so a storage device with both SAS and iSCSI ports can use the same identifier on both, simplifying management and making the device naming consistent across protocols.
sections.eli5: When a storage device has multiple kinds of connections, it is easier if they all use the same ID number.

sections.title: Naming Across SCSI Transports
sections.content:
Different SCSI transports use different naming schemes:

  • iSCSI: Originally supported EUI-64 and IQN formats only.
  • Fibre Channel (FC): Uses NAA format.
  • Serial Attached SCSI (SAS): Uses NAA format.
  • SRP (SCSI RDMA Protocol for InfiniBand): Uses EUI-64 format.

NAA is the most common format in deployed SCSI transports today, since both FC and SAS devices typically use it. Adding NAA support to iSCSI brings it into alignment with industry practice.
sections.eli5: Different storage connections have their own naming styles. This adds a common style to iSCSI.

sections.title: iSCSI NAA Name Format
sections.content:
An iSCSI node name using the NAA format begins with the prefix naa. followed by the NAA identifier represented as ASCII-encoded hexadecimal digits.

Example NAA names:

  • 64-bit NAA: naa.52004567BA64678D
  • 128-bit NAA: naa.62004567BA64678D0123456789ABCDEF

The NAA identifier is at most 32 hexadecimal characters (128 bits), so it always fits within iSCSI's maximum node name size. Implementations typically use this format when they already have infrastructure for generating NAA identifiers (for example, in a device that also has SAS ports).
sections.eli5: The format is simple: write 'naa.' and then the ID number in hex. A 128-bit ID is at most 32 characters, so it fits easily in iSCSI names.

sections.title: NAA Identifier Structure
sections.content:
The NAA identifier structure is defined by INCITS T11 Fibre Channel standards. It provides a way to construct globally unique identifiers using various identifier registration authorities. The NAA format supports different subtypes and is widely used in FC and SAS implementations.

By reusing this format for iSCSI, administrators can leverage existing tooling, identifier assignment infrastructure, and documentation that already exist for FC and SAS devices. A storage device with both SAS and iSCSI ports can now report the same worldwide unique identifier to initiators on both transports, as required by INCITS T10 SCSI standards.
sections.eli5: NAA is a standard way to create unique IDs that works across many storage technologies. Using it in iSCSI means less work for device makers and less confusion for administrators.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The NAA naming format does not introduce any new security concerns for iSCSI beyond those of the other naming formats (EUI-64 and IQN). The format is simply a way to identify a device by a unique number; the security properties of iSCSI itself (authentication, encryption, access control) are unchanged.

Administrators should refer to RFC 3720 (the iSCSI specification) for detailed security considerations on iSCSI protocol.
sections.eli5: Giving a device a different kind of name does not make iSCSI less secure.
